- When sentiment is strongly bullish (≥0.67) and forecast is trending upward, reduce forecast slope to avoid over-optimism; if sentiment turns bearish, increase downward bias.
- After sharp price spikes (e.g., >5% from prior day), model tends to overshoot — apply a 1–2 day lag correction to prevent overreaction.
- If sentiment history shows repeated bearish signals (e.g., 3+ consecutive 0.33 or lower), model often underestimates downside — add 0.5–1.0 to forecast mean to counteract mean reversion bias.
- In low-sentiment or neutral periods (sentiment ≤0.33), model often underpredicts volatility — increase forecast variance or add 0.5–1.0 to mean to account for hidden risk.
- When true outcome deviates >3% from 30d forecast mean, check if sentiment shifted sharply — if yes, adjust forecast to align with sentiment direction, not just historical trend.
- For 30d horizon, if true outcome is >10% above forecast mean, consider sentiment as “strongly bullish” — adjust next forecast to reflect momentum decay (e.g., reduce slope by 10–20%).
- If sentiment is mixed or volatile (alternating 0.33–1.00), model often overfits short-term noise — apply smoothing filter or reduce forecast amplitude by 5–10% to avoid overfitting.
